160	Moses our teacher set apart three across the Jordan, and Joshua set apart three in the land of
161	Canaan.
162	But the Torah has an explicit mitzvah, and the Torah is eternal, that when HaShem expands your border
163	and you add three more cities, so that in the end there should be nine cities of refuge, and where
164	will the three additional cities be? In the lands of Keni, Kenizi and Kadmoni.
165	When will this be, says the Rambam, as practical law: "And in the days of the King Mashiach, three others are added
166	to the six."
167	Where are they added, says the Rambam, all as practical law? In the lands of Keni, Kenizi and Kadmoni.
168	That means that in HaShem's mitzvah, the mitzvah of setting apart cities of refuge, which overall should have
169	nine cities of refuge, something is still missing from the mitzvah as a whole.
170	So the completeness of the possession of the land of Israel is also lacking, even of the seven lands, and the Rebbe wants to prove
171	that even by the simple meaning, as long as we have not conquered or received openly
172	the last three lands, which are Keni, Kenizi and Kadmoni, the whole possession of
173	the land of Israel is lacking.
174	Even though, from HaShem's side, everything was given at once.
175	So if...
176	In the Rebbe's wording and terminology: from HaShem's side
177	the giving is not only as a promise but also an actual giving, because HaShem's
178	speech is deed.
179	But it is still not open and revealed.
180	For it to be open and actual, or in the phrase the Rebbe often uses, "in actuality and openly,"
181	it depends on things being done not only from above to below, from HaShem's side, but also
182	from the side of the reality below.
183	What characterizes HaShem's giving?
184	That it is all at once, like speech.
185	Speech is all at once, so too the giving is all at once.
186	What characterizes the realization of things from below upward?
187	That it comes specifically in stages, because anything that must happen from within, from below upward, must
188	come in stages, like the simple analogy.
189	A person can jump from the top of the roof down in one jump, but if he wants
190	to go up from below to above, it cannot be done in one jump; he must climb the stairs.
191	Even if a person wants to give up his life, he cannot jump from the ground to the roof.
192	For the order is that from below, it must come in stages, and the inner reason is so that it
193	will belong to the person's own powers, to the limits of the lower realms.
194	The person's limit, the limit of the lower realms in general, is a limit.
195	And within a limit, it is impossible to do the whole matter at once.
196	It must be stage after stage.
197	So we see that even in the most fundamental matter of Judaism,
198	expressed in the most fundamental matters of the parashah, which is Lech Lecha and the promise of the land, we have
